summary: Defines how a router gets validated route-origin data (which Autonomous System may announce which address block) from a trusted cache that has already checked the RPKI cryptography. Routers stay simple because they never do the heavy certificate checking themselves; they just fetch the results.

eli5.summary: A router needs a list of who owns which street address. Instead of checking every deed itself, it asks a trusted helper who already checked them, and gets a short, simple list.

subtitle: How a router fetches already-validated route-origin data from a trusted cache over a simple binary protocol.

tldr.problem: Routers need verified information about which Autonomous System may originate which prefix, but they cannot be expected to do the heavy RPKI cryptography themselves.
tldr.mechanism: A trusted cache validates the RPKI data and serves it to routers over a persistent session using a handful of small binary PDUs, with serial numbers for incremental updates and a session ID to keep both sides in step.
tldr.outcome: Routers get compact prefix-origin records they can use for BGP origin validation. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8210.

facts.label: Serial Notify rate limit
facts.value: No more than one per minute

today: RFC 6810 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8210, so read that RFC alongside it. The text here describes protocol version 0 and says its error code list is preliminary.

sections.title: Why Routers Need a Cache
sections.content:
To verifiably validate the origin Autonomous Systems of BGP announcements, routers need RPKI prefix origin data that has been cryptographically validated. This RFC defines the RPKI-to-Router protocol, which delivers that data from a trusted cache to routers.

The design is intentionally constrained so that it can run on much of the then-current generation of ISP router platforms. The protocol is extensible: new PDUs with new semantics can be added, and PDUs are versioned should deployment experience call for change.
sections.eli5: Checking every deed is slow and hard work. So a helper does the checking and the router just reads the helper's short list.

sections.title: Three Levels: Global RPKI, Caches and Routers
sections.content:
Deployment has a three-level structure. The Global RPKI is the authoritative data, published in a distributed set of repositories run by bodies such as the IANA, the RIRs, NIRs and ISPs. Local caches collect and verify that data. Routers are clients of a local cache and fetch from it using this protocol.

A relying party such as a router MUST have a trust relationship with, and a trusted transport channel to, any authoritative cache it uses. The RFC also defines two counters that tie the pieces together. The Serial Number is a 32-bit strictly increasing unsigned integer, wrapping from 2^32-1 to 0, that denotes the logical version of a cache. The Session ID is generated when a cache starts and binds the cache instance to the sequence of serial numbers it produces.

If either side finds that the Session ID is not the same as the other's, they MUST completely drop the session and the router MUST flush all data learned from that cache. Cache clocks MUST be correct to a tolerance of approximately an hour, because certificates and ROAs are time dependent.
sections.eli5: There is a big library of deeds, a local helper who copies and checks them, and your router, who only talks to the helper. A ticket number tells the router whether the helper's list is still the same one it saw before.

sections.title: The Protocol Data Units
sections.content:
Every PDU starts with an 8-bit Protocol Version (currently 0) and an 8-bit PDU Type, followed by a 32-bit Length that counts the whole PDU. Fields with unspecified content MUST be zero on transmission and MAY be ignored on receipt.

The router-to-cache PDUs are Serial Query (ask for everything newer than a Serial Number) and Reset Query (ask for the full current database). The cache sends Serial Notify, Cache Response, End of Data, Cache Reset and the payload PDUs. Serial Notify is the only message the cache can send that is not in response to a message from the router.

The payload is carried by the IPv4 Prefix and IPv6 Prefix PDUs. Each holds a Flags field (lowest bit 1 for an announcement, 0 for a withdrawal), a Prefix Length, a Max Length, the prefix and an Autonomous System Number. Max Length MUST NOT be less than Prefix Length. The cache MUST ensure that the router holds one and only one such PDU for a unique {Prefix, Len, Max-Len, ASN} at any one time.
sections.eli5: The router and helper only use a few kinds of short notes: "anything new?", "here is a record", "that is all", and "start over". Each note has a label on the front saying what kind it is.

sections.title: How Routers and Caches Talk
sections.content:
When a transport session is first established, the router MAY send a Reset Query, and the cache answers with a Cache Response, zero or more prefix PDUs and an End of Data PDU carrying the new serial. If the router has significant unexpired data from a broken session with the same cache, it MAY instead start with a Serial Query containing the Session ID from the previous session.

In steady state, the cache SHOULD send a Serial Notify when its serial changes, and MUST rate limit these to no more than one per minute. The notify is only a hint. A router MUST send either a Serial Query or a Reset Query no less frequently than once an hour, which also acts as an application-layer keep-alive.

If the cache cannot supply an incremental update from the router's serial, it replies with a Cache Reset. The router SHOULD try any more preferred caches, and if there are none it MUST issue a Reset Query and take a full load. If the cache has no data at all, it sends an Error Report with code 2 (No Data Available). The router SHOULD try other caches in preference order, and otherwise MUST issue periodic Reset Queries until it gets a usable load.
sections.eli5: The router asks "what has changed since ticket number 5?" If the helper has lost track, it says "start over" and gives the whole list. The router also checks in at least once an hour so the helper knows it is still there.

sections.title: Error Reports
sections.content:
Either party can send an Error Report PDU, but only as a response to another PDU, and an Error Report MUST NOT be sent for an Error Report. The PDU carries an Error Code, an optional copy of the offending PDU and optional UTF-8 diagnostic text.

The RFC lists a preliminary set of eight codes, and says errors considered fatal SHOULD cause the session to be dropped. Withdrawing a record the receiver does not have (code 6) and announcing a record it already holds (code 7) are both fatal. These checks let a router notice that it has fallen out of step with its cache.
sections.eli5: If a note makes no sense, you can send back a note saying what went wrong. You never send a complaint about a complaint.

sections.title: Router-Cache Setup and Deployment
sections.content:
A router is configured with a list of caches, each with a preference value (lower is more preferred), a name, any needed public key of the cache and any needed private key or certificate of its own. The preference denotes proximity, not trust. The router tries each cache in preference order and loads from the most preferred one it can connect to and authenticate.

A client may hold data from several caches but MUST keep it marked by source, and when validating, implementations MUST NOT distinguish between data sources. A client SHOULD delete a cache's data if it cannot refresh from it for a configurable time, whose default is twice the polling period. When switching caches it SHOULD keep the old data until it has a full set from another.

Three illustrative scenarios are given: a small end site outsourcing a cache to its upstream ISPs, a larger site running a hierarchy of caches, and an ISP backbone with redundant caches in each major point of presence. The RFC warns that complex cache topologies are ill-advised, and recommends that primary caches avoid fetching from the Global RPKI all at the same time, for example on the hour.
sections.eli5: A router keeps a ranked list of helpers to ask, nearest first. It keeps the old list until it has a full new one, so it is never left with nothing.

sections.title: Transport and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says it is highly desirable that router and cache authenticate each other, but because there is no protocol that works on all platforms, there is no mandatory-to-implement transport that provides authentication and integrity protection. It is expected that TCP-AO will become mandatory-to-implement once it is available everywhere.

Caches and routers MUST implement unprotected TCP on port rpki-rtr (323). If unprotected TCP is used, the cache and router MUST be on the same trusted and controlled network. Where available, they SHOULD use TCP-AO, SSHv2, TCP MD5 or IPsec, and MAY use TLS on port rpki-rtr-tls (324). SSH runs the protocol as a subsystem named rpki-rtr. With TLS, routers MUST present client certificates and MUST verify the cache's server certificate.

The RPKI relies on object trust, but this protocol assumes routers cannot do the validation cryptography. The last hop is therefore secured by server authentication and transport security, which have very different threat models. The RFC puts it bluntly: you are betting your routing on this link.
sections.eli5: The router trusts the helper's list completely, so it must be sure it is really talking to the right helper, and nobody can sneak in a fake list on the way.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Lowest bit is 1 for an announcement and 0 for a withdrawal.

fields.name: Autonomous System Number
fields.desc: The ASN allowed to announce this prefix.

items.label: Serial Notify
items.desc: Cache hints that it has new data.

items.label: Serial Query
items.desc: Router asks for changes after a serial.

items.label: Reset Query
items.desc: Router asks for the full database.

items.label: IPv4 Prefix
items.desc: Announce or withdraw an IPv4 prefix record.

items.label: IPv6 Prefix
items.desc: Announce or withdraw an IPv6 prefix record.

items.label: End of Data
items.desc: Cache has no more data, and sends the new serial.

items.label: Cache Reset
items.desc: Cache cannot give an incremental update.

messages.label: Serial Notify
messages.note: Optional hint that new data exists.

messages.label: Serial Query
messages.note: Router requests data newer than its serial.

items.label: Corrupt Data
items.desc: PDU believed corrupt in a way no other code covers. Fatal.

items.label: Internal Error
items.desc: Reporter had an internal problem. Fatal.

items.label: No Data Available
items.desc: Cache has no useful data yet; likely temporary.

items.label: Invalid Request
items.desc: Cache believes the client's request is invalid. Fatal.

items.label: Unsupported Protocol Version
items.desc: Receiver does not know the version. Fatal.

items.label: Unsupported PDU Type
items.desc: Receiver does not know the PDU type. Fatal.

items.label: Withdrawal of Unknown Record
items.desc: Withdraw for a record that is not held. Fatal.

items.label: Duplicate Announcement Received
items.desc: Announce of a record that is still active. Fatal.
